hints_cache: This is a shortest-path problem in disguise. Since every jump (left, right, or teleport) counts as exactly one step, think about which traversal method explores all '1-step' options before moving to '2-step' options.

To handle the 'teleport' rule efficiently, you need a way to instantly find all indices that share the same value. A Hash Table mapping each number to a list of its positions will save you from scanning the whole array every time.

Standard Breadth-First Search (BFS) will work, but the 'Hard' part is the performance. If you're at an index with the value '100', you'll look up all other '100's in your map and add them to your search queue.

Here is the trick: once you have processed all teleport destinations for a specific value (like '100'), you will never need to 'teleport' from that value ever again. If you don't find a way to skip those redundant checks, your search will be too slow.

Start BFS at index 0, using a queue to track your current index and step count. For each index, explore its neighbors (i+1, i-1) and all teleport indices from your map, then immediately clear that entry in the map so you don't re-process those same jumps from a different starting point.
